target_customer: iOS app teams and mobile product teams buying SwiftUI component libraries
problem: Teams spend design and engineering time rebuilding common app components that handle styling, localization, accessibility and platform conventions.
business_model: Paid component library for teams with demos and sales, plus open source Pow library for awareness

founders.name: Robb Böhnke
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him as Founder with a one line bio. A Crunchbase search result and a personal bio call him co-founder and CEO.

founders.name: Michael Nino Evensen
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page. No education or employers given.

technical_complexity.rationale: High quality SwiftUI components that handle accessibility, localization and dark mode need deep platform knowledge, but they are application level code rather than new technology.

defensibility.rationale: Component code is copyable and distributed to customers; the open source Pow library built reputation among iOS developers.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No source found on Apple or others copying the components.

market_need_then: SwiftUI was a young framework in 2021 with few polished component sets, and the company site shows testimonials from objc.io, Rapha Racing, Sedna Systems and Kraken Exchange. No dated spend data was found.

identity.visual_style: Product demo style site with components such as checkout cart and card entry form.
identity.voice_and_tone: YC page calls the components delightful; founder bio reads I like short bios.

branding.brand_signature: Pow open source SwiftUI transitions library
branding.community_and_virality: Pow was open source and a Substack review called Moving Parts and Pow favorites; the site shows Mastodon, Twitter and Instagram links.

brand_strength.rationale: Small developer following through Pow and a few testimonials, but little press and a generic name.

outcome_analysis: Moving Parts was a two person Berlin team selling polished SwiftUI components that also released the open source Pow library. YC marks it Inactive, but the site still loads with a newest article from January 2023 and no shutdown notice or acquisition was found, so the cause is not public and no failure factors are assigned. Only a pre-seed of about 130 thousand dollars is known, and the small paid market for UI components is a plausible limit that no source confirms.
notes: Funding rests on Seedtable, an aggregator; another Seedtable page lists 125K over 2 rounds, Clera lists 120K and Dealroom a 125K seed, so the amount is unverified. No investors listed by those sources; the site names Y Combinator, Haystack and Notion as supporters. Article bylines Robb and Kasper appear on the site; Kasper is not recorded as a founder. No dated competitor source near 2021 was found, so the list is empty.
